caldera.notes: Generator: TerrainField's crater lowers the summit but never below its own edge (the centre stands at 0.88 of the cone's height, the edge at 0.845), so the top is a flattened dome, not a bowl, and holds no water; it is also only about one blueprint cell across (0.7-1.4 km geographic against cells of about 1 km). HydrologyPass fills every closed basin to its spill level whatever the rain (only hot, dry basins go salt), so a closed caldera becomes the crater_lake variant; a floor to live on needs a notch in the rim that drains it, or a lake level set lower by hand in dry country. BiomePass makes every land cell within 0.45 of a cone's radius HOT_SPRING or VOLCANIC_FIELD; the caldera floor should take its climate's grass or forest, with HOT_SPRING only at the vents. In cold, high country the floor is a summer place (the Valles Caldera's warm-season camps), and an obsidian_flow can sit on it.

obsidian_flow.name: Obsidian flow
obsidian_flow.when: On the upper slopes of a land volcano or on a caldera's floor, where a late, thick, silica-rich lava cooled too fast to grow crystals: a short, steep-fronted flow of black glass.

cause.other: land cones only, never a sea hotspot; one or two flows on a few cones, by seed

obsidian_flow.shape: A thick tongue of lava ending in a steep front a few storeys high, built of black and banded glass blocks; its top a jumble of glassy boulders and ridges. At the foot, a fan of broken glass that glitters in low sun. Nothing grows on the fresh glass; lichen and a few pines on the older edges.
obsidian_flow.hearth_spot: Off the glass, on flat ground 30-50 m from the foot of the flow front, beside the nearest spring or stream; the knapping floor lies between the hearth and the glass fan, where blocks are carried to be worked.
obsidian_flow.hazard: Glass: blocks and fan have razor edges and slide underfoot; a fall on the flow cuts.

links.roads: a node like a spring: trails from far camps lead to it, and toolstone walks out along them (the exchange rung)
links.audio: footsteps on the glass fan clink

real_world.note: Quarried for toolmaking for more than 11,000 years, its glass is found along old trade routes from western Canada to the Great Lakes and Ohio.

Obsidian from Obsidian Cliff and from Idaho, more than 2,400 km from the nearest volcano, was shaped into large ceremonial spear points, probably carried in by people who travelled to the source or by visitors coming to the ceremonies.
Hunting, gathering plants and collecting obsidian for stone tools were the main reasons people came up for short warm-season stays, over nearly eight thousand years.

obsidian_flow.notes: Obsidian comes from silica-rich lava (rhyolite), not basalt; the engine's volcanic rock is all basalt, so the flow is a seeded set piece on the cone, not a rock type. Inside the cone core BiomePass only makes VOLCANIC_FIELD or HOT_SPRING; on a caldera floor the flow takes the floor's dressing (the Valles Caldera's obsidian lies on the flanks of its forested domes, above grass valleys). Mountain, desert and shelter folk teach obsidian_knapping (techniques.json); the knapping floor is its ruin.

volcanic_neck.name: Volcanic neck
volcanic_neck.when: On flat, dry, open country far from the live cones: where an old volcano's throat of hard rock outlasted the soft rock around it, a lone tower stands up from the plain.
volcanic_neck.shape: A lone tower or crag of dark rock, sheer-walled or in tall columns, 20-50 m high in the game (200-500 m Earth-equivalent) and narrower at the top than at the foot; a skirt of fallen blocks round its base; low, straight walls of the same dark rock (dikes) running out across the plain from it for hundreds of metres. The footprint is kept narrow for its height so it reads as a tower, not a mound. On this planet (radius about 637 km) a 20-50 m tower drops below the horizon beyond about 6.5-9.5 km for someone standing on flat ground, and shows further from a hill: the tallest thing on that skyline.
volcanic_neck.hearth_spot: Not on the tower: at the nearest spring or creek within sight of it, in the lee of a dike or of the tower's downwind foot, at least 100 m out from the fallen blocks.
volcanic_neck.hazard: Rockfall: blocks and columns break off the sheer walls into the skirt at the foot.

links.roads: a landmark the trails steer by, like a standing stone
links.rooms: framed in a reveal from a ridge or valley edge

real_world.region: Navajo Nation, Four Corners region, New Mexico
real_world.note: The eroded throat of a volcano, about 480 m high with wall-like dikes radiating from it, it holds a large place in Navajo religion and tradition, and its name, rock with wings, recalls the great bird that brought the Navajo from the north.

More than two dozen tribes are tied to the Tower, which they know as Bear Lodge, Bear's Tipi and other names: a sacred place of winter camps, vision quests and summer ceremonies, where prayer cloths still hang in the trees.

Magma that cooled about 1.6 to 3.2 km underground some 50 million years ago began to be laid bare by erosion 5 to 10 million years ago, and geologists still debate whether it fed a volcano or never reached the surface.

volcanic_neck.notes: The engine has only the nine live cones; a neck is the root of an old one worn away, so it is a seeded tower on open plains with no cone around it (hotspot old). Shiprock is a true neck; Devils Tower's origin is still debated (a plug, a laccolith, a stock or a diatreme), but both are hard igneous rock left standing by erosion. Both are sacred to the peoples around them, and the Navajo Nation has banned climbing on Shiprock since 1970: the tower is for the long view, not for climbing. To be seen past the walking chunks it needs a far form (FarShell or a vista impostor).

mesa.name: Mesa and butte
mesa.when: Dry sandstone country where the escarpment lines close into islands: the ground inside stands as a flat table above the flats, in two or three cliff steps, and rain soaking down through the top seeps out at the foot of the caprock.

cause.other: inside the escarpment mask (TerrainField), where a cliff line closes into an island

variants.name: Tepui
variants.when: The same table of hard, flat-lying rock in hot, wet country, raised far higher: sheer cliffs on every side, a cool summit wet with cloud, waterfalls pouring off the rim. Phase 2: nothing is classified TEPUI until this landform exists.
variants.note: A landmark more than a home. WORLD_SYSTEMS_SPEC puts it on sandstone, which GeologyPass makes only below moisture 0.3, so the tepui needs its own rock rule.

mesa.shape: A flat-topped table of rock, wider than tall, with sheer sides over a skirt of fallen blocks. A hard caprock makes the rim, softer banded rock lies below; two or three cliff steps of escarpment height (about 14 m each) with ledges between. Shallow arched alcoves open at the foot of the caprock where water seeps out. Worn further, a table becomes buttes, taller than wide, and then thin spires, standing apart on the flats.
mesa.hearth_spot: In a seep alcove at the foot of the caprock: the fire on the dry front of the alcove floor, a few metres inside the drip line, with the seep and its basin against the back wall. A camp on top sits at least 10 m back from the rim, at the head of the one trail.
mesa.hazard: The rim and the ledge edges: a sheer drop of a full cliff step; blocks fall from the caprock onto the talus below.

links.roads: the seep is a node, like a spring; the one trail up is the only road onto the top
links.threshold: stairs: the one way up, steps cut in the rock, then footholds
links.gate: cliff: off the rim is one way; the trail is the only way back up
links.rooms: the alcove is a roofed room with one feature, the seep

real_world.region: about 97 km west of Albuquerque, New Mexico, USA
real_world.note: Acoma Pueblo stands on a mesa about 110 m high that has sheltered its people for centuries; in 1540 the only way up was a hand-built stair and then footholds in the rock, and cisterns on top caught snow and rain.

Water soaks down through the sandstone to the shale below and seeps out along it, where damp and frost carve the alcoves; with no permanent streams on the mesa, the Ancestral Pueblo people drew water from these seeps, cutting small basins in the shale to pool it.

real_world.analogue: The tepuis of Canaima National Park
real_world.note: Table mountains cover about two thirds of the park, with sheer cliffs and waterfalls, among them the world's highest at about 1,000 m.

mesa.notes: The escarpment noise already lifts some closed islands by ESCARP_M (TerrainField._cliffs): in dry sandstone, key those as mesas, add a second and third step at higher noise levels, and let the smallest islands stand as buttes and spires. The alcove is a mesh on the cliff face (roof_rule), like camps.gd's cliff slab. Sandstone exists only below moisture 0.3 (GeologyPass), so shortgrass gets mesas only at its dry edge. Peoples.pick gives every cliff site to shelter folk, but Mesa Verde's alcoves were farmers' homes (rock_shelter.json says so too): a mesa rule should put desert folk first. Mesa country, many tables together, is the region version.

plants.where: The hanging garden: maidenhair along the wet seep line at the back of an alcove.

dunes.name: Dunes, barchan and booming
dunes.when: Dry country with loose sand on a flat floor and one steady wind (a strong mean wind in the cell), inland or on a dry coast: crescent dunes stand apart on the bare floor, horns pointing downwind.

cause.other: loose sand on a hard, flat floor; the horns point down the cell's mean wind (wind_avg)

variants.name: Parabolic dunes
variants.when: The same sand and steady onshore wind on a coast damp enough for grass: the grass pins the dunes' arms, so they become U-shapes with the arms trailing upwind, behind a grassy foredune along the beach.
variants.note: Coast folk camp dug into the lee of the foredune, out of the onshore wind, with the beach in front for food.

dunes.shape: Crescents of bare sand standing apart on a hard, flat floor, each wider than long: a gentle windward back with ripples, a steep slip face (about 30-35°) in the hollow of the crescent, and two horns reaching downwind. Up to about 30 m high. Where sand is plentiful they join into long ridges across the wind.
dunes.hearth_spot: Off the sand: on the hard floor just upwind of the field, a short walk from the gentle back of the first crescent, never under a slip face. Where a spring rises in a deep hollow among the dunes, on the hollow's floor well out from the slopes (that is the oasis nest).
dunes.hazard: Losing the way: every crest looks alike and no road crosses; the slip face slides underfoot.

links.audio: the booming dune, a new SOURCE kind (§BG): a loud droning hum, near 450 Hz, for as long as its slip face slides, set off by the wind or by walking the crest; loud enough to walk toward, silent when wet
links.roads: roads skirt a dune field rather than cross it

real_world.analogue: Mingsha Shan (Echo Sand Mountain) and Crescent Lake
real_world.note: Mingsha is known as the singing dunes for the noise the wind makes in its sand, and its dunes surround the 100 m long Crescent Lake near Dunhuang, the oasis where the Silk Roads split around the Taklamakan.

real_world.region: about 35 desert sites worldwide, among them Mingsha Shan, the Namib and the Kelso Dunes in California
real_world.note: Round, dry silica sand avalanching down a dune, set off by the wind or by someone walking near the crest, can boom at up to 105 dB for several minutes, while wet sand is usually silent.

real_world.region: deserts and sandy coasts on Earth; Mars
real_world.note: Crescent dunes, the commonest dune on Earth and Mars, form under wind from one direction with the slip face in the hollow of the crescent, while parabolic dunes, well known in coastal deserts, have arms that trail upwind because plants hold them while the bulk of the sand moves on.

dunes.notes: Aim each crescent by wind_avg at its cell: the slip face and horns face down the mean wind. Baked at generation (§BS): the dunes never move in play. One dune per field, the tallest and driest, booms (links.audio). A spring in a hollow among the dunes is the oasis nest, as at Crescent Lake. Inland there is no sand soil (dry country is sandstone, GeologyPass), so the field is a stamp. BiomePass makes DUNES only on a coast with moisture under 0.3, though the DUNES template runs 0.2-0.8; the parabolic variant needs that rule widened. A whole sand sea (erg) is the region version.

salt_flat.name: Salt flat
salt_flat.when: A closed basin in dry country that loses more water to the sun than it gets, so its lake has dried to a salt crust (a SALT_FLAT cell); the nest is the spot on its rim where a spring or stream brings fresh water in.

cause.other: a closed basin that evaporates more than it gets (today: a salt lake under 350 mm of rain and above 8 °C); the nest is where a spring or stream reaches the rim

salt_flat.shape: A dead-flat white crust kilometres across on the floor of a closed basin, cracked into raised-rim polygons a few metres across. At the rim, where a spring or stream comes in, a green fringe of saltgrass and glasswort and a shallow run of fresh water fading into the salt; bare desert slopes all round. After rain, a thin film of still water lies on it and mirrors the sky.
salt_flat.hearth_spot: On firm ground at the rim, just above the wet-season water line, beside the spring or stream where fresh water comes in; the salt workings lie out on the crust in front of it.
salt_flat.hazard: Out on the crust: no water, no fuel, no shade and a white glare; after rain the mirror hides the way.

links.roads: the dry crust is itself a road across the basin, closed when it floods; the rim spring is a node, like a spring
links.magic: never a glow pond: MagicSites skips salt lakes

real_world.note: The world's largest salt flat, about 10,600 km², is mined by the salt workers of the Colchani cooperative and is a main route across the Altiplano except when the wet season floods it; after rain, a thin film of still water makes it a mirror 129 km across.
Each year Quechua herders of the high puna carried salt from the salares of Uyuni and Coipasa down to the valleys by llama caravan and bartered it for maize, chili, wood and coca.

real_world.analogue: Taoudenni salt mine and its caravans
real_world.note: Miners cut slabs of salt of about 30 kg from the bed of an ancient salt lake, and camel caravans carry four or five slabs per camel some three weeks south to Timbuktu.

salt_flat.notes: Today a SALT_FLAT cell is drawn as a salt lake (open water). The flat wants a dry white crust with polygon cracks most of the year (a look), and the mirror film only after rain, read from the weather (dressing only, §BS). The salt-lake rule needs a basin mean above 8 °C (hydrology_pass SALT_LAKE_MIN_TEMP_C), so no salt lake forms in the puna band (-3 to 5 °C) or the colder half of the cold desert; lower it to give the puna its salars. Peoples.pick: the lake site rule takes any lake shore, salt ones too, so a rim camp gets lake folk unless this nest gets its own rule ahead of it. Salt is desert folk's exchange rung (the last step of their ladder: salt out on the road, pots, grain and fish back), and their salt_pan technique is the work done here. Desert folk have no ruin signature for old salt workings yet (cut-block pits, a stack of salt cakes); coast's salt_pans are cut in shore rock.

oasis.name: Oasis
oasis.when: Desert or thorn scrub where groundwater reaches the surface: a spring at the foot of an escarpment, or a pool in a hollow deep enough to reach the water table (today's OASIS: a fresh lake where moisture is under 0.25).

cause.other: groundwater at the surface: a spring at an escarpment's foot, a pool in a deep hollow (among dunes too), or a fresh lake in desert (today's OASIS cells)

oasis.shape: A spring or pool where groundwater comes up at the foot of a cliff or in the floor of a deep hollow, ringed by date palms, tamarisk, reeds and sedge: a dark green island in bare sand or stone. Lived in, it becomes a three-storey garden: palms on top, fruit trees under them, vegetables and grain below a metre, watered by channels from the spring into small basins.
oasis.hearth_spot: Beside the spring head, on dry, stony ground just off the watered land, in the shade of the outer palms; the channels run from the spring past the camp down to the plots.

links.roads: a node, like a spring; caravan roads run oasis to oasis
links.rooms: one feature: the spring head under the palms
links.magic: the pool can be one of the glow ponds (MagicSites: fresh lakes)
links.audio: water_flow at the spring head and in the channels

real_world.note: The Siwans, of Berber ancestry, water their gardens from natural springs by gravity in small basins, and the garden grows in three storeys: date palms on top, fruit trees in the middle and other crops under a metre high.
Ten oases are strung along 75 km on the lee side of a 100 m escarpment, where groundwater is easy to reach, famous for salt and dates and once a stop on the Bornu to Fezzan caravan trail.

real_world.region: Iran, spread across Asia and North Africa
real_world.note: Developed in ancient Iran about 3,000 years ago and called foggara in Algeria, a qanat is a gently sloping tunnel, reached by a line of vertical shafts, that leads groundwater out to the surface far away with little lost to the sun.

oasis.notes: Today an OASIS cell is any fresh lake where moisture is under 0.25 (BiomePass). New: the spring at the foot of an escarpment that crosses desert (a road node, the OASIS dressing around it), and the pool in a hollow among dunes (Crescent Lake, see dunes). Where the water lies far off under the hills, a qanat taps it and leads it out to the garden: desert folk's technique, not the player's, and its line of shafts is the ruin (qanat_shafts). Peoples.pick: the lake site rule takes any lake shore, so an oasis lake gets lake folk unless this nest gets its own rule ahead of it.

bog_and_fen.name: Bog and fen
bog_and_fen.when: Flat, waterlogged, cool ground where dead plants pile up as peat because the water keeps them from rotting. A bog is fed by rain alone: acid, spongy, sphagnum moss, no stream in. A fen is fed by groundwater and streams: richer water, sedge and reed, alder at its rim. Nobody lives on it: the nest is the first firm rise at its edge, or an island built in its open water (a crannóg).

variants.name: Reed island
variants.when: The same flat, waterlogged ground in warm country, where the game lays no peat (above 14 °C): reed marsh or swamp. The island is still built, of reed and mud, and the boat is the road.
variants.note: Marsh folk's house islands: new reed laid on the old mound.

bog_and_fen.shape: A wide, flat sheet of moss and sedge with dark pools, cottongrass and a few stunted pines (bog), or a tall sea of reed and sedge with alder thickets round it (fen). At the edge, a low knoll or ridge of firm ground. Out in open water, a small round island 8-25 m across, built up of timber, brush, clay, peat and stone inside a ring of piles: the crannóg, reached by log boat or a causeway. A trackway of planks on crossed pegs runs out from the edge across the wet.
bog_and_fen.hearth_spot: On the first firm rise of mineral ground at the edge (a till knoll, a sand ridge or an old river terrace), 20-50 m back from where the peat begins, at the landward end of the trackway; or in the middle of a built island, on a hearth of clay and flat stones laid over the timber.
bog_and_fen.hazard: The open bog: quaking moss over deep, water-filled peat that swallows a leg, and pools that look like ground. Off the trackway, nobody walks on it.

links.roads: a new road kind, the trackway: planks on crossed pegs from the edge to the island or across to the next dry ground (marsh folk's trackway technique)
links.threshold: the trackway's landward end, read as a bridge
links.magic: bog and fen pools are among MagicSites' glow ponds

real_world.note: In 3807 BC, by tree-ring date, people laid about 1,800 m of oak planks on crossed poles across the marsh between an island at Westhay and the high ground at Shapwick, and used it for about ten years.

real_world.region: lochs, lakes and bogs of Ireland and Scotland
real_world.note: Partly or wholly artificial islands, often ringed with timber piles and built up of clay, peat, stone, timber or brush, lived on over five thousand years, from the Neolithic to the 1600s or early 1700s.

real_world.region: the Tigris–Euphrates marshes, southern Iraq; a living people
real_world.note: Houses stood at the water's edge or on islands of piled reed (kibasha), or, to last longer, of layered reed and mud (dibin).

bog_and_fen.notes: Generator: BiomePass splits them by water, FEN beside a river or lake and BOG away from both; GeologyPass's alluvium rule comes before clay_peat, so every fen sits on alluvium, and clay_peat lies under bogs and other flat, wet, cool ground away from water. The game's BOG and FEN (-7 to 5 °C) are colder than the Somerset Levels or the Irish bogs; there the same cause, flat waterlogged peat, lands in WET_MEADOW or FRESHWATER_MARSH (peat below 14 °C), so those are dressings too. The Sweet Track is the second-oldest timber trackway found in the British Isles.

levee_and_chenier.name: Natural levee and chenier
levee_and_chenier.when: Along a big, silty river winding across a flat floodplain: each flood drops its coarsest silt where it spills over the bank, building a low ridge along both banks, higher and drier than the swamp behind. In flat, wet country it is the one dry line.

variants.name: Chenier
variants.when: On a flat, muddy coast where waves once heaped shell and sand into a beach ridge and the shore then built out in mud in front of it: an old beach ridge stranded in the marsh, running parallel to the shore, under live oaks in Louisiana, among the coastal swamps between the Amazon and the Orinoco.
variants.note: The same one dry line in salt country, built on first because it stands above the floods.

levee_and_chenier.shape: A low, broad bank along each side of the river, highest at the water's edge (1-3 m above the swamp behind it) and sloping gently away into the backswamp. Firm, well-drained silt, so it carries the big trees and the trail while the land behind stays wet. Where a flood broke through, a fan of sand spreads out into the swamp.
levee_and_chenier.hearth_spot: On the levee's crest, the highest strip, 10-30 m back from the river's cut bank (which can slump), with the boats pulled up on the bank below and the backswamp behind; the houses string out along the crest, not across it.
levee_and_chenier.hazard: A big flood can top the levee or break through it and fill the backswamp; the cut bank slumps into the channel.

links.roads: the crest is the road along the river (roads.json follow_rivers), and camps string out along it
links.rooms: the rooms at bends and confluences sit on it

real_world.region: Gulf Coast of Louisiana, from Sabine Lake to Vermilion Bay
real_world.note: Cheniers are sandy or shelly beach ridges between mudflats and marsh, named for their groves of live oak, and when the region was settled they were built on by preference because their height kept them above the floods.
High levees along the Euphrates let water flow by gravity to the fields around, and breaks in them (crevasse splays) spread it over the floodplain.

real_world.region: Greater Upper Nile, South Sudan, and Gambella, Ethiopia; a living people
real_world.note: When the heavy rains come they move their cattle up to the higher ground, in part to keep them from hoof disease.

levee_and_chenier.notes: Two twins of one nest: the levee, from river silt, and the chenier, an old beach ridge (the variant). BiomePass already finds the big-river flat (FLOODPLAIN_FOREST: flat, beside a river above the big-river discharge, moisture over 0.5); in drier country the same flat dresses as SAVANNA or HOT_DESERT. The levee is a walking-scale raise along that river's banks. River folk already build on the natural levee above the flood (river.json dressing). Where no levee is high enough, people built their own high ground: the river folk's mound.

beaver_pond.name: Beaver pond
beaver_pond.when: On a small stream in a gentle, wooded valley with willow, aspen, birch or alder on the banks: beavers dam the stream with sticks and mud, and the water backs up over the valley floor. When the trees run out or the pond silts up they leave; the dam breaks and the pond drains to a meadow.

cause.other: a small stream, not a big river, with trees beavers eat on its banks

beaver_pond.shape: Active: a curved dam of sticks, mud and stones across the stream, a metre or two high and from a few metres to about 100 m long; behind it a still pond over the valley floor, drowned trees standing grey in it, a domed lodge of sticks out in the water, chewed stumps and felled trunks along the banks, and channels dug out into the wood. Abandoned: the dam breached, the pond drained to a flat meadow of grass and sedge with the stream winding through it and the grey snags still standing.
beaver_pond.hearth_spot: On firm, higher ground at one end of the dam, a few metres above the pond and out of the stream bed below it; the dam is the camp's footbridge. Abandoned: at the meadow's edge, under the first trees.
beaver_pond.hazard: Soft, sucking mud and drowned logs at the pond's edge, and the stream bed below the dam, which takes the water if the dam goes.

links.roads: the dam is a ford node
links.rooms: the pond is a room's one feature, open sky over drowned trees
links.audio: water_flow at the dam: a trickle through the sticks

real_world.analogue: Beaver clearings in the eastern forests
real_world.note: Beaver ponds opened clearings in the forest whose fish, waterfowl and big game drew Native American and early colonial hunters, and before the fur trade there were perhaps 100 to 200 million beavers, against 10 to 15 million today.

When a pond silts up or the trees run out the beavers leave, the dam is breached and drains, and the wetland left behind can become a meadow; each cycle adds a layer of soil to the valley floor and widens it.

real_world.region: Nitassinan, the Labrador Peninsula; a living people
real_world.note: They hunted beaver alongside caribou, moose, bear and fish, and the fur trade, the focus of their dealings with Europeans for two centuries, did them great harm, because trapping left no room to follow the caribou.

beaver_pond.notes: Two states, baked at generation (§BS) and picked by seed: active (dam whole, pond full, fresh-cut stumps, the lodge) and abandoned (dam breached, meadow, grey snags). No live change: nothing rebuilds the dam during play. Generator: only the top few percent of discharge becomes a river and RiverNetwork draws them 7-55 m wide, while beavers dam small streams, so the pond goes on the narrowest headwater reaches or on a side stream drawn just for it. The pond is a walking-scale water plane, like the plunge pools, not a blueprint lake.

columnar_basalt.name: Columnar basalt
columnar_basalt.when: Where a thick, old lava flow cooled slowly and cracked into hexagonal columns, and water has since laid them bare: a flat stepped floor of column tops running down into the sea on a volcanic coast (the causeway); a cliff of columns where a river or a fall has cut the flow (the organ pipes); a cave the sea has hollowed in the flow (the columned sea cave).

cause.other: An old flow, not a live cone: the columns are laid bare only where the sea or a river has cut into the flow. The causeway needs a volcanic coast; the organ pipes a river or a fall through basalt country; the sea cave a cliff coast of basalt facing open sea.

columnar_basalt.shape: The causeway: a field of close-packed hexagonal columns of dark grey-black basalt, 30-50 cm across, their tops at stepped heights so the whole reads as a stair of flat stones going down into the sea; the tops hold rain and tide pools with green weed in the cups; the columns stand 6-12 m tall at the landward edge and vanish under the water at the seaward one. The organ pipes: the same columns standing 10-40 m tall in a cliff face, a fall pouring over them where a river cuts the flow. The sea cave: a cave hollowed into the column cliff, the roof the underside of the columns, the sea running in, and a ledge of broken column stumps along one wall above the water to the back. Dark grey-black with wet tops (navy shade); a hexagon tile at 16 texels a metre does the work.
columnar_basalt.hearth_spot: The causeway: on the highest dry step above the spray, in the lee of the cliff. The organ pipes: at the foot of the cliff by the pool, out of the spray. The sea cave: never inside (no dry floor); on the clifftop above it.
columnar_basalt.hazard: The sea: the lower steps are awash at high water and in a swell; the sea cave fills to the ledge in a storm; wet column tops are slick.

links.roads: the causeway reads as a road of stone steps going down into the sea, and the coast road runs to its top (§BC: the player finishes the thought)
links.rooms: the sea cave is a corridor with the sea as its floor and the mouth as its only light
links.audio: the sea cave booms with the swell, a source heard from the clifftop before the way down is found (§BG); the wind moans in the organ pipes above 6 m/s (§DA)

variants.name: Organ pipes
variants.when: A river or a waterfall has cut through the flow inland: a cliff of columns 10-40 m tall, the fall pouring over them.
variants.note: The waterfall nest's basalt dressing; the hearth spot is at the foot by the pool.

variants.name: Columned sea cave
variants.when: The sea has hollowed the column cliff: the roof is the underside of the columns, the sea runs in, and a ledge of column stumps along the wall is the way to the back.
variants.note: Never a camp (no dry floor): a landmark and a passage; the night roster dens in it (§CH); the hearth spot is on the clifftop.

real_world.note: About 40,000 interlocking basalt columns from a lava flow some 50-60 million years ago, mostly hexagonal, their tops forming stepping stones that lead from the cliff foot and disappear under the sea; the legend has the giant Finn McCool build it as a road to Scotland.

A sea cave formed entirely of hexagonally jointed basalt columns, about 20 m high and 70 m deep, with a natural walkway of fractured column tops along the wall just above the sea; its arched roof and the swell give it an echo that drew Mendelssohn to write his overture.
A waterfall pouring over a cliff of dark basalt columns, the organ-pipe form; the columns inspired the architecture of Reykjavik's Hallgrímskirkja.
A 20 m wall of columnar basalt from a lava flow about 82,000-100,000 years ago, later planed by a glacier so its top is a floor of polished hexagons.

columnar_basalt.notes: Design 3 Oct §DX (Mike: a cool natural formation). The columns come loose, so the people who lived here built with them: a hut of stacked hexagonal columns is the camp's remains, a coast-folk signature to add with the next peoples fill (not listed in remains until it exists). The log line, once: 'A road of stone steps goes down into the sea.' Walking scale (§CK): the columns are true size.
